title: The Home Guard stands down

facts.text: The Home Guard began in May 1940 as the Local Defence Volunteers, raised against German parachute landings if Britain was invaded. It was soon renamed the Home Guard at Winston Churchill's insistence.
More than 1.5 million local volunteers joined over the course of the war.
On 31 October 1944 the War Secretary, Sir James Grigg, told the Commons it had been decided to stand the Home Guard down. King George VI wished every member to receive a certificate signed by him.

The Home Guard stood down on Sunday 3 December 1944, with final parades across the country. An amateur film at the Imperial War Museum records the last parade of the 1st Loyal City of Exeter Battalion that day.
In Hyde Park about 7,000 officers and men, representing every Home Guard unit in Britain, marched past the King, their Colonel in Chief. The Queen and the two princesses stood with him.
That evening the Home Guard held a Stand Down party at the Royal Albert Hall, with the comedians George Robey and Tommy Trinder on stage.
At 9 p.m. the King broadcast his thanks. Press reports said he spoke of the comradeship this citizen army had built, and his belief that it would help to solve the problems of peace.
The Home Guard never fought the invasion it was raised for, but it was not without cost: 1,206 members were killed on duty or died of wounds, many from bombs and rockets.
The same autumn Germany went the other way. On 25 September 1944 Hitler ordered the Volkssturm, a militia of males from 16 to 60, to be thrown into the last battles.
The Home Guard was formally disbanded on 31 December 1945.

photoNote: Tier: green. Friday cards run, 27 Nov 2026: no stand down photo could be fetched (IWM blocks the workspace; Commons has none), and the bank holds only off date Axis Spec Sheets, so the card uses IWM H 2936 from Wikimedia Commons (1280 px thumbnail): the King with Home Guard volunteers in Kent, 10 August 1940, a related photo from four years earlier, said plainly in the credit and caption. Flagged to Brian; if he supplies an IWM H series photo of the Hyde Park parade, swap it in. Research's original note: PHOTO NOT FETCHED. Tier: green when found. Wanted: an IWM War Office official photograph (H series, Crown copyright expired, not an HU press number) of the Hyde Park stand down parade, 3 December 1944, ideally the King taking the salute or a close column of older Home Guards marching past. The IWM site sits behind a Cloudflare check that blocks both the shell and WebFetch, and I found no stand down photo on Wikimedia Commons (its Home Guard category holds IWM H numbers only up to H 39707, July 1944). Leads to check on iwm.org.uk: War Office official photos H 40953, H 40954 (dated 1 December 1944), H 40956 and H 40957 (object pages 205216344, 205216345, 205216347, 205216348), which surfaced in a search for the stand down but whose captions could not be read; the Hyde Park parade itself should sit just after them in the H 409xx to H 410xx range. Do not use the Geoff Charles Welshpool stand down photos on Commons (National Library of Wales, CC BY SA 4.0, not green) or the 14 May 1944 anniversary parade photos often mixed up with the stand down. Fallback if no H photo turns up: a frame from the Universal Newsreel of 27 December 1944 on Commons (NARA, public domain), which shows the Hyde Park march past.

declassified.fact: Section Commander George Inwood of the Birmingham Home Guard won the George Cross after a raid on the night of 15 October 1940. Lowered by rope into a gas filled cellar in Bishop Street, he brought out two men and was overcome on his third trip down. He died on 16 October 1940.

sources.title: Section Commander George Walter Inwood, Commonwealth War Graves Commission

body:
More than 1.5 million Britons volunteered to fight an invasion that never came. On this Sunday they paraded for the last time.

3 December 1944. The Home Guard stood down with final parades across the country. In Hyde Park about 7,000 officers and men, from every unit in Britain, marched past King George VI, their Colonel in Chief, with the Queen and the two princesses beside him. At 9 p.m. the King broadcast his thanks.

It was not without cost: 1,206 members were killed on duty or died of wounds, many from bombs and rockets. That same autumn Germany went the other way, ordering males from 16 to 60 into the Volkssturm.

Above, the King with Home Guard volunteers in Kent, August 1940.
